questions.question: Which of the following steps can increase the expected yield of a crop?

options.text: Irrigation at early stages of crop.
Irrigation at right stage of crop.
Irrigation at terminal stage of crop.
Irrigation at every stage of crop.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Irrigation at right stage of crop**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **expected yield** of any crop is highly dependent on the availability of water at specific physiological periods known as **Critical Growth Stages**. Providing water at the **right stage** ensures that the plant does not undergo moisture stress during vital development phases. ***Hence, the correct option is Irrigation at right stage of crop.***
 
• **Irrigation at early stages** of the crop is important for seed **germination** and seedling establishment, but if subsequent critical stages are neglected, the overall **yield** will drop significantly. *Hence, statement 1 is only partially beneficial.*
 
• **Irrigation at the right stage** refers to identifying the periods when the plant is most sensitive to water deficits, such as **flowering**, **fruiting**, or **grain filling**. Applying water during these windows maximizes **productivity** and resource efficiency. *Hence, statement 2 is correct.*
 
• **Irrigation at the terminal stage** (the final phase of the crop cycle) might help in maturing the seeds, but it cannot compensate for water stress experienced during the **reproductive phase**. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect as a standalone measure to increase yield.*
 
• **Irrigation at every stage** of the crop is often counterproductive and leads to **waterlogging**, which deprives roots of **oxygen**, increases the risk of **fungal diseases**, and wastes water resources. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Critical Irrigation Stages for Various Crops**:
 
 
• **Wheat**: The most critical stage is the **Crown Root Initiation (CRI)**, which typically occurs **21 days after sowing**. Other stages include tillering, flowering, and milk stage.
 
• **Rice**: Critical stages include the **panicle initiation**, **flowering**, and **heading** stages where moisture is vital for grain count.
 
• **Maize**: The **tasseling** and **silking** stages are highly sensitive to water stress.
 
• **Pulses**: These crops generally require irrigation at the **flower initiation** and **pod development** stages.
 
 
 
• **Irrigation Scheduling**: It is the process of deciding **when to irrigate** and **how much water** to apply. This is based on **soil moisture** levels, **evapotranspiration** rates, and the specific **growth stage** of the crop.
 
• **Water Use Efficiency (WUE)**: This is a measure of a crop's ability to convert water into biomass or **yield**. Effective **irrigation management** at the **right stage** improves the **WUE**, ensuring sustainable **agriculture**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact of Over-Irrigation**: Excessive water application leads to **leaching of nutrients**, **salinity** build-up in the soil, and reduced **soil aeration**, all of which negatively impact the final **yield**.
 
• **Precision Irrigation**: Technologies like **Drip Irrigation** and **Sprinkler Systems** allow farmers to apply water precisely at the **right stage** and in the correct **quantity**, reducing **water wastage** by up to **40-50%**.
 
• **Soil Type Influence**: The timing of irrigation also depends on **soil texture**; for example, **sandy soils** require more frequent irrigation compared to **clayey soils** due to lower water-holding capacity.
 
• **Climate Factors**: High **temperatures** and low **humidity** increase the plant's **transpiration** rate, requiring more frequent checks on whether the crop has reached a **critical stage** for water.
</ul

questions.question: A straight conductor is carrying current in the +x-direction, this conductor is placed in a magnetic field pointing in the +y-direction. What will be the direction of motion of the conductor?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**positive z direction**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When a **straight conductor** carrying an **electric current** is placed within an external **magnetic field**, it experiences a mechanical **force**. This phenomenon is a fundamental principle of **electromagnetism**.
 
• The **direction** of this force is always **perpendicular** to both the direction of the **current** and the direction of the **magnetic field**.
 
• The relationship between these vectors is defined by the **Lorentz Force** equation, expressed as **F = I (L × B)**, where **F** is the force vector, **I** is the current, **L** is the length vector in the direction of current, and **B** is the magnetic field vector.
 
• In this specific problem, the **current** is moving in the **+x-direction** (represented by the unit vector **i**) and the **magnetic field** is oriented in the **+y-direction** (represented by the unit vector **j**).
 
• By applying the mathematical **cross product** rules for **Cartesian coordinates**, we find that **i × j = k**. Since **k** represents the **positive z-axis**, the resulting motion of the conductor will be in the **positive z direction**. ***Hence, the statement is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fleming's Left-Hand Rule**: This is a practical mnemonic used to find the **direction** of **force** acting on a conductor. If you stretch the **thumb**, **forefinger**, and **middle finger** of your left hand so they are mutually **perpendicular**:
 
 
• The **Forefinger** represents the direction of the **Magnetic Field**.
 
• The **Middle finger** represents the direction of the **Current**.
 
• The **Thumb** points in the direction of the **Force** or **Motion**.
 
 
 
• **Magnitude of Magnetic Force**: The amount of force experienced by the wire depends on the **current (I)**, the **length (L)** of the wire, the strength of the **magnetic field (B)**, and the **sine** of the **angle (θ)** between the current and the field. The formula is **F = BIL sinθ**.
 
• **Right-Hand Palm Rule**: Another method where the **fingers** point in the direction of the **field** and the **thumb** points in the direction of the **current**; the **palm** then pushes in the direction of the **magnetic force**.
 
• **Applications**: This principle is the working basis for **Electric Motors**, where **electrical energy** is converted into **mechanical energy**. It is also used in **galvanometers**, **loudspeakers**, and **magnetic levitation** systems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Maximum Force**: The **conductor** experiences the **maximum force** when it is placed **perpendicular** (at an **angle** of **90 degrees**) to the **magnetic field lines**. In this orientation, **sin 90° = 1**.
 
• **Zero Force**: If the **conductor** is placed **parallel** or **anti-parallel** to the **magnetic field** (at an **angle** of **0 or 180 degrees**), the **force** exerted on it is **zero** because **sin 0° = 0**.
 
• **Force on Moving Charges**: The force on a single **charge (q)** moving with a **velocity (v)** in a **magnetic field** is given by **F = q(v × B)**. A **current-carrying wire** is simply a collection of many such moving charges.
 
• **Newton’s Third Law**: Just as the **magnetic field** exerts a **force** on the **current-carrying wire**, the wire also exerts an equal and opposite **magnetic force** on the source of the magnetic field (such as a **permanent magnet**).

questions.question: The principle of conservation of energy is applicable to __________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**every physical process in general**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Law of Conservation of Energy** is a fundamental principle of physics which states that the **total energy** of an **isolated system** remains **constant**; it is said to be conserved over **time**.
 
• Energy can neither be **created nor destroyed**; rather, it can only be **transformed** or transferred from one form to another. For instance, in a falling object, **potential energy** is converted into **kinetic energy**.
 
• The principle is applicable to **every physical process in general** because energy is a universal currency in all interactions, whether they are **mechanical**, **electrical**, **chemical**, **thermal**, or **nuclear**. ***Hence, option 4 is correct.***
 
• Options 1, 2, and 3 are incorrect because they use restrictive terms like **"only"** or **"exclusively."** While the law applies to **mechanical**, **electrical**, and **chemical** systems, it is not limited to them. ***Hence, statements 1, 2, and 3 are incorrect.***
 
• In any transformation, if we account for all forms of energy—including those dissipated as **heat**, **sound**, or **friction**—the sum remains the same.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **First Law of Thermodynamics:** This is a specific version of the conservation of energy principle applied to **thermodynamic systems**. It states that the change in **internal energy** of a system is equal to the **heat** added to the system minus the **work** done by the system.
 
• **Forms of Energy:** Energy exists in various forms such as **Mechanical** (Kinetic and Potential), **Thermal** (heat), **Chemical** (stored in bonds), **Electrical** (moving charges), **Radiant** (light), and **Nuclear** (stored in the nucleus of an atom).
 
• **Energy Transformation Examples:**
 
 
• In a **battery**, **chemical energy** is converted into **electrical energy**.
 
• In an **electric motor**, **electrical energy** is converted into **mechanical energy**.
 
• In **photosynthesis**, plants convert **solar energy** into **chemical energy**.
 
 
 
• **Mass-Energy Equivalence:** In modern physics, **Albert Einstein** expanded this principle through the formula **E = mc²**, which suggests that **mass** and **energy** are interconvertible. This is particularly relevant in **nuclear reactions** (fission and fusion) where a small amount of mass is converted into a huge amount of energy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Isolated System:** A system that does not exchange **matter** or **energy** with its surroundings. The **universe** itself is often considered the ultimate isolated system where total energy is constant.
 
• **Noether’s Theorem:** In theoretical physics, the conservation of energy is a mathematical consequence of **time-translation symmetry**. This means that the **laws of physics** do not change with **time**; therefore, energy must be conserved.
 
• **Perpetual Motion Machines:** The law of conservation of energy confirms that a **perpetual motion machine of the first kind** (a machine that produces work without energy input) is **physically impossible**.
 
• **Efficiency:** While energy is always conserved, it is not always conserved in a **useful form**. In most real-world processes, some energy is "lost" as **waste heat** due to **entropy**, though it still exists within the total system energy count.

questions.question: Which meristem is located near the nodes in some plants?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Intercalary meristem**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Intercalary meristems** are specifically located at the **base of leaves** or **internodes** (near the **nodes**) in certain plants.
 
• These tissues are essentially **portions of the apical meristem** that have been separated from the apex by the development of **permanent tissues** during the growth process.
 
• They play a crucial role in the **elongation of the plant body** and are responsible for the **longitudinal growth** of the internodes.
 
• In **grasses** and other **monocots**, the intercalary meristem allows for the **regrowth of stems and leaves** after they have been damaged or consumed by **herbivorous animals**.
 
• Unlike apical meristems which are at the tips, the intercalary meristem provides a mechanism for growth within the **middle regions** of the plant structure.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Apical Meristem**:
 
 
• Located at the **growing tips** of **roots** and **shoots**.
 
• It is responsible for the **increase in the length** of the plant, a process known as **primary growth**.
 
• It helps the plant explore more **soil** for water and reach higher for **sunlight**.
 
 
 
• **Lateral Meristem**:
 
 
• Found on the **lateral sides** of the stems and roots, running parallel to the long axis.
 
• It facilitates **secondary growth**, which results in an **increase in the girth** or thickness of the plant.
 
• Examples include the **vascular cambium** and the **cork cambium** (phellogen) in woody plants.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Meristematic Cells**:
 
 
• The cells are **actively dividing** and are usually **small**, **isodiametric**, or **spherical** in shape.
 
• They possess **thin cellulose cell walls**, **dense cytoplasm**, and a **prominent nucleus**.
 
• These cells generally lack **vacuoles** because they are focused on **multiplication** rather than storage or structural support.
 
 
 
• **Root Meristem**:
 
 
• Specifically refers to the **apical meristem** located at the **root apex**.
 
• It is often protected by a **root cap** to prevent damage as the root pushes through the **soil**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Classification**: Meristems are classified based on their **position** in the plant body into three primary types: **Apical**, **Intercalary**, and **Lateral**.
 
• **Linguistic Context**: The word "meristem" is derived from the **Greek word 'meristos'**, which means **divisible**, highlighting the tissue's capacity for **continuous cell division**.
 
• **Growth Cycles**: While **primary meristems** (Apical and Intercalary) appear **early in the life** of a plant, **secondary meristems** (Lateral) usually appear **later** to provide structural thickness.
</ul

questions.question: What is the formula of washing soda?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Na2CO3.10H2O**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Washing soda** is a chemical compound with the formula **Na2CO3.10H2O**. Its chemical name is **sodium carbonate decahydrate**.
 
• It is a **crystalline solid** that contains **ten molecules** of **water of crystallization** attached to one molecule of **sodium carbonate**. ***Hence, option 4 is correct.***
 
• It is produced via the **Solvay process**, where **sodium chloride**, **ammonia**, and **carbon dioxide** react to form **sodium hydrogen carbonate**, which is then heated and recrystallized.
 
• Washing soda is a **basic salt**, meaning it forms an alkaline solution when dissolved in water, turning red litmus blue.
 
• The **anhydrous** form of this compound (without water) is known as **soda ash** or **sodium carbonate** (**Na2CO3**). ***Hence, option 3 is incorrect*** as it lacks the hydration necessary for washing soda.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH):**
 
 
• Commonly known as **caustic soda**, it is a strong **base** used in the manufacture of **soaps**, **detergents**, **paper**, and **synthetic fibers** like **rayon**. ***Hence, option 1 is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Sodium Hydrogen Carbonate (NaHCO3):**
 
 
• Commonly known as **baking soda**, it is used in the food industry for baking and as an **antacid** to treat indigestion. It also acts as a primary component in **soda-acid fire extinguishers**. ***Hence, option 2 is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Uses of Washing Soda:**
 
 
• It is primarily used in the **glass**, **soap**, and **paper industries**.
 
• A major application is the removal of **permanent hardness** of water, which is caused by dissolved **calcium** and **magnesium** salts.
 
• It is used in the manufacturing of sodium compounds like **borax** and serves as a vital **cleansing agent** for domestic laundry purposes.
 
 
 
• **Chemical Properties:**
 
 
• When exposed to air, **washing soda** undergoes **efflorescence**, losing nine molecules of water to form **sodium carbonate monohydrate** (**Na2CO3.H2O**).
 
• It is highly soluble in water and its solution is **alkaline** in nature, which aids in cutting through grease and stains during cleaning.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **History:** The **Solvay process** was developed in the **1860s** by **Ernest Solvay**, revolutionizing the industrial production of **sodium carbonate**.
 
• **Water of Crystallization:** This refers to the fixed number of water molecules that form part of the structure of a **crystal**. In washing soda, there are exactly **10** such molecules.
 
• **Environmental Impact:** Washing soda is considered more environmentally friendly than many synthetic detergents as it is **biodegradable** and does not contain **phosphates** that lead to **eutrophication**.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is a basic requirement for maintaining good reproductive health?

options.text: Safe sex practices and awareness about contraception

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Safe sex practices and awareness about contraception**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Reproductive health** is defined by the **World Health Organization (WHO)** as a total well-being in all aspects of reproduction, including **physical**, **emotional**, **behavioral**, and **social** dimensions.
 
• Maintaining **safe sex practices** is a fundamental requirement as it prevents the spread of **Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)** such as **syphilis**, **gonorrhea**, **genital herpes**, and life-threatening diseases like **HIV/AIDS**.
 
• **Awareness about contraception** is essential for **family planning**, allowing individuals to decide the number and spacing of their children, which directly impacts the **socio-economic status** of a family and the nation. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• Sharing **personal hygiene products** (like towels or undergarments) is highly discouraged as it can lead to the transmission of **fungal infections**, **skin diseases**, and **UTIs**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• Monitoring and understanding the **physical and hormonal changes** during **adolescence** is vital for mental health and early detection of reproductive issues. Ignoring these changes can lead to **anxiety** or **undiagnosed medical conditions**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Medical intervention** and the use of prescribed **medicines** (such as **antibiotics** for infections or **hormonal therapy**) are often necessary to maintain reproductive health; thus, avoiding all medicines is counterproductive. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Adolescence and Puberty**:
 
 
• **Adolescence** is the period of life between **10 to 19 years** when the body undergoes changes leading to **reproductive maturity**.
 
• During **puberty**, the **testes** and **ovaries** begin to produce **gametes** (sperm and ova) and **hormones** like **testosterone** (in males) and **estrogen/progesterone** (in females).
 
 
 
• **Menstrual Hygiene**:
 
 
• Maintenance of **cleanliness** during the **menstrual cycle** is crucial to prevent **bacterial infections** and **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)**.
 
• The use of **sanitary napkins** or clean **menstrual cups** and changing them every **4-6 hours** is a standard health recommendation.
 
 
 
• **Nutritional Needs**:
 
 
• A **balanced diet** containing **Iron** (to prevent **anemia**), **Calcium**, and **Proteins** is particularly important for **pregnant women** and **adolescent girls** to support reproductive functions.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives**:
 
 
• In **India**, the **Reproductive and Child Health (RCH)** program was launched to create awareness and provide medical facilities for **maternal health**, **infant mortality reduction**, and **birth control**.
 
• The **legal age for marriage** in **India** (currently **18 for females** and **21 for males**) is also designed to ensure that individuals are **physiologically** and **mentally** prepared for reproduction.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Amniocentesis**: This is a medical technique used to determine **chromosomal abnormalities** in the fetus. However, its misuse for **sex determination** led to a **statutory ban** in **India** under the **Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994**.
 
• **Population Explosion**: Lack of **reproductive health awareness** leads to rapid population growth. Methods like **IUCDs (Intrauterine Contraceptive Devices)**, **Oral Pills**, and **Surgical Methods** (**Vasectomy** and **Tubectomy**) are tools used to stabilize population growth.
 
• **Lactational Amenorrhea**: A natural method of **contraception** where **ovulation** does not occur during the period of **intense lactation** following childbirth, though it is only effective for a maximum of **six months**.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of judicious use of natural resources?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rainwater harvesting**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Judicious use** of **natural resources** refers to the **sustainable** and **efficient management** of resources to meet present needs without compromising the ability of **future generations** to meet their own needs.
 
• **Rainwater harvesting** is a method of **water conservation** where **precipitation** is collected and stored for later use, rather than being allowed to run off. It helps in **recharging groundwater** levels and reduces the burden on **municipal water supplies**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Open mining** (also known as open-pit mining) involves the **extraction of minerals** from an open pit in the ground. This process often leads to significant **environmental degradation**, **habitat destruction**, and **soil erosion**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Excessive use of fossil fuels** like **coal**, **petroleum**, and **natural gas** leads to the **depletion of non-renewable resources** and increases **carbon emissions**, contributing to **global warming**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• **Deforestation** is the **permanent removal of trees** to make room for something besides forest. This results in **loss of biodiversity**, disruption of the **water cycle**, and increased **atmospheric carbon dioxide**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Rainwater harvesting.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Natural Resources:** 
 
 
• These are substances that occur naturally within **environments** that exist relatively undisturbed by mankind, in a natural form.
 
• They are classified into **Renewable Resources** (e.g., **solar energy**, **wind**, **water**) which can be replenished naturally over time, and **Non-renewable Resources** (e.g., **minerals**, **fossil fuels**) which exist in finite amounts and take **millions of years** to form.
 
 
 
• **Sustainable Development:** 
 
 
• This concept was popularized by the **Brundtland Commission** in **1987**. It emphasizes the **judicious use** of resources to maintain **ecological balance**.
 
• Methods include practicing the **3Rs**: **Reduce**, **Reuse**, and **Recycle** to minimize **waste generation** and **resource consumption**.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct in the context of a mixture and a compound?

A) A mixture has a variable composition while in a compound, the composition of each new substance is always fixed.
B) A mixture shows the different properties of the constituent substance while in a compound, the new substance shows the same properties.
C) A mixture has a non-variable composition while in a compound, the composition of each new substance is always changing.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only A**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement A:** In a **mixture**, the **composition** of the **constituent substances** is **variable**, meaning they can be mixed in any **proportion**. Conversely, a **compound** is a substance formed when two or more **elements** chemically combine in a **fixed ratio** by **mass**, and the **composition** of each **new substance** is always **fixed**. ***Hence, statement A is correct.***
 
• **Statement B:** A **mixture** reflects the **physical properties** of its **constituent substances** because they are not **chemically bonded**. However, in a **compound**, the **new substance** formed has entirely **different properties** from its **constituent elements**; it does not show the **same properties** as the **atoms** it is made of. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• **Statement C:** This statement suggests that a **mixture** has a **non-variable composition** and a **compound** has a **changing composition**. This is **factually incorrect** as it contradicts the **fundamental laws of chemistry**, specifically the **Law of Constant Proportions**, which states that **compounds** always have a **definite composition**. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Only A.***

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mixtures:**
 
 
• A **mixture** is a **physical combination** of two or more **substances** that are not **chemically linked**.
 
• **Types:** They are classified into **homogeneous mixtures** (uniform **composition**, like **saltwater** or **air**) and **heterogeneous mixtures** (non-uniform **composition**, like **sand and iron filings**).
 
• **Separation:** The **constituents** of a **mixture** can be separated using **physical methods** such as **filtration**, **evaporation**, **distillation**, or **magnetism**.
 
• **Energy:** Usually, no **energy** (in the form of **heat** or **light**) is **absorbed** or **evolved** during the formation of a **mixture**.
 
 
 
• **Compounds:**
 
 
• A **compound** is a **pure substance** made of **atoms** of two or more **elements** **chemically bonded** together.
 
• **Formation:** The formation of a **compound** involves a **chemical reaction**, often accompanied by the **evolution** or **absorption** of **energy**.
 
• **Separation:** The **constituents** of a **compound** can only be separated by **chemical** or **electrochemical reactions**; **physical methods** do not work.
 
• **Examples:** **Water (H2O)** is a **compound** of **hydrogen** and **oxygen**. **Methane (CH4)** and **Common Salt (NaCl)** are other common **examples**.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison of Properties:**
 
 
• In a **mixture** (e.g., **iron** and **sulfur** powder mixed), **iron** retains its **magnetic properties**.
 
• In a **compound** (e.g., **Iron Sulphide**), the **iron** loses its **magnetic properties** because a **new chemical substance** has been formed.
 
 
 
• **Melting and Boiling Points:**
 
 
• **Compounds** typically have **fixed melting points** and **boiling points** due to their **fixed composition**.
 
• **Mixtures** do not have **sharp melting or boiling points**; they melt or boil over a **range of temperatures** depending on the **ratio** of **constituents**.
 
 
</ul

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Potassium, Gold**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Reactivity Series** (also known as the activity series) is an arrangement of metals in **descending order** of their chemical reactivity. It helps in predicting how metals will react with water, acids, and other metal salts.
 
• **Potassium (K)** is placed at the very top of the reactivity series, making it the **most reactive metal**. Due to its high reactivity, it reacts vigorously with **oxygen** and **water** even at room temperature.
 
• **Gold (Au)** is placed at the bottom of the reactivity series, making it the **least reactive metal**. It is often referred to as a **noble metal** because it does not react with air, water, or most acids under standard conditions.
 
• The general order of the series from high to low reactivity is: **Potassium (K) > Sodium (Na) > Calcium (Ca) > Magnesium (Mg) > Aluminium (Al) > Zinc (Zn) > Iron (Fe) > Tin (Sn) > Lead (Pb) > [Hydrogen (H)] > Copper (Cu) > Mercury (Hg) > Silver (Ag) > Gold (Au)**.
 
• Metals like **Magnesium** and **Sodium** are also highly reactive but are placed below Potassium. **Silver** is less reactive than Copper but more reactive than Gold.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• Because it reacts explosively with water to produce **Hydrogen gas** and heat, it must be stored under **kerosene** or **paraffin oil** to prevent contact with moisture and air.
 
• It has a very **low ionization energy**, meaning it loses its single valence electron very easily to form **K+ ions**.
 
 
 
• **Gold (Au)**:
 
 
• It is a **Transition Metal** with **atomic number 79**.
 
• It is highly **malleable** and **ductile**, and its resistance to **corrosion** and oxidation makes it ideal for **jewelry** and **electronic components**.
 
• It is often found in nature in its **native state** (pure form) because it does not readily form compounds with other elements.
 
 
 
• **Magnesium (Mg)** and **Silver (Ag)**:
 
 
• **Magnesium** (Atomic number **12**) reacts with boiling water or steam but is less violent than Potassium.
 
• **Silver** (Atomic number **47**) is used in coinage and photography; while it tarnishes in the presence of sulfur, it is still significantly less reactive than base metals.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Displacement Reactions**: A more reactive metal (like **Potassium** or **Zinc**) can displace a less reactive metal (like **Copper** or **Silver**) from its oxide or salt solution.
 
• **Hydrogen Reference**: **Hydrogen** is included in the series as a reference point. Metals placed **above Hydrogen** can displace it from dilute acids to release hydrogen gas, whereas metals **below Hydrogen** (like Copper, Silver, Gold) cannot.
 
• **Extraction Methods**: The reactivity of a metal determines its extraction method. **Highly reactive metals** (Potassium, Sodium, Calcium) are extracted via **electrolysis** of their molten chlorides, while **moderately reactive metals** (Zinc, Iron) are reduced using **carbon** (coke).
 
• **Electropositivity**: Reactivity is directly related to **electropositivity**. Potassium is the most electropositive element in this context, having the strongest tendency to lose electrons and form **positive ions**.
</ul

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**non-uniform motion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Non-uniform motion** is defined as a type of motion where an object covers **unequal distances** in equal intervals of time. In the case of a freely falling stone, its **velocity** increases continuously as it descends due to the pull of **gravity**. ***Hence, option 1 is correct.***
 
• A stone falling under the influence of **gravity** alone (ignoring air resistance) experiences a **constant acceleration** known as **acceleration due to gravity (g)**, which is approximately **9.8 m/s²** on the surface of the **Earth**.
 
• Since the **speed** of the stone is not constant and increases every second by **9.8 m/s**, it cannot be classified as **uniform motion** or **rectilinear motion with constant speed**. ***Hence, options 2 and 4 are incorrect.***
 
• Because there is a definite **force** (gravitational force) acting on the stone, it possesses a specific **acceleration**. Therefore, the motion does not have **zero acceleration**. ***Hence, option 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The path of the stone is a **straight line**, making it a **rectilinear motion**, but because the magnitude of the **velocity** changes, it is specifically categorized as **uniformly accelerated non-uniform motion**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Uniform Motion**:
 
 
• An object is said to be in **uniform motion** if it moves along a **straight line** and covers **equal distances** in equal intervals of time, regardless of the duration of the time intervals.
 
• In this state, the **acceleration** of the body is **zero** and the **velocity** remains **constant** throughout the journey.
 
 
 
• **Acceleration due to Gravity (g)**:
 
 
• It is the **acceleration** gained by an object due to the **gravitational force** of a massive body like **Earth**.
 
• The standard value of **g** is **9.80665 m/s²**. This value varies slightly depending on **latitude**, **altitude**, and the **geological structure** of the region.
 
• It is a **vector quantity**, always directed towards the **center** of the planet.
 
 
 
• **Rectilinear Motion**:
 
 
• This refers to motion in a **straight line**. It can be of two types: **Uniform Rectilinear Motion** (constant velocity) and **Non-Uniform Rectilinear Motion** (changing velocity/accelerated).
 
• A falling stone is an example of **Non-Uniform Rectilinear Motion**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Equations of Motion for Free Fall**:
 
 
• When an object is dropped from **rest** (initial velocity **u = 0**), the equations of motion simplify to: **v = gt**, **h = 1/2 gt²**, and **v² = 2gh**.
 
• In these equations, **v** is the final velocity, **t** is the time taken, and **h** is the height or **displacement**.
 
 
 
• **Mass Independence**:
 
 
• In a **vacuum** (where **air resistance** is absent), all objects fall with the same **acceleration (g)** regardless of their **mass** or **shape**. This was famously demonstrated by **Galileo Galilei**.
 
 
 
• **Terminal Velocity**:
 
 
• In a real atmosphere, as an object falls, **air resistance** increases with **speed**. Eventually, the upward air resistance equals the downward weight, and the object stops accelerating, moving at a **constant speed** called **terminal velocity**.

questions.question: When an object is placed between the pole (P) and the focus (F) of a concave mirror, what kind of image is formed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Virtual, erect, and enlarged**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **concave mirror** is a spherical mirror with a reflecting surface that curves **inward**, resembling the interior of a bowl. It is also known as a **converging mirror** because it converges light rays that fall on it.
 
• When an object is placed between the **pole (P)** and the **principal focus (F)** of a concave mirror, the rays of light originating from the object **diverge** after reflection.
 
• Because the reflected rays are diverging, they never meet on the side of the object. Instead, they appear to meet at a point **behind the mirror** when traced backward. This results in the formation of a **virtual image**.
 
• The image formed in this specific position is **erect** (upright) and **enlarged** (magnified), meaning the size of the image is greater than the size of the object. ***Hence, the correct answer is Virtual, erect, and enlarged.***
 
• This is a unique case for a concave mirror because, for all other object positions (such as at F, between C and F, at C, or beyond C), the image formed is **real and inverted**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Common Uses:** Due to its ability to form an **enlarged and erect** image when the object is close, this property of the concave mirror is utilized in **shaving mirrors** and **makeup mirrors** to see a larger view of the face. **Dentists** also use concave mirrors to see large images of the teeth of patients.
 
• **Image Formation at Other Positions:**
 
 
• **At Infinity:** The image is formed at the **focus (F)**, and it is **real, inverted**, and **highly diminished** (point-sized).
 
• **Beyond Center of Curvature (C):** The image is formed between **F and C**, and it is **real, inverted**, and **diminished**.
 
• **At Center of Curvature (C):** The image is formed **at C**, and it is **real, inverted**, and the **same size** as the object.
 
• **Between C and F:** The image is formed **beyond C**, and it is **real, inverted**, and **enlarged**.
 
• **At Focus (F):** The image is formed at **infinity**, and it is **real, inverted**, and **highly enlarged**.
 
 
 
• **Convex Mirrors:** Unlike concave mirrors, **convex mirrors** always form a **virtual, erect, and diminished** image, regardless of the object's distance from the mirror. They are widely used as **rear-view mirrors** in vehicles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mirror Formula:** The relationship between object distance (**u**), image distance (**v**), and focal length (**f**) is given by **1/f = 1/v + 1/u**.
 
• **Magnification (m):** It is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object (**m = h'/h**). It is also expressed as **m = -v/u**.
 
 
• In the case of an object between **P and F**, the magnification is **positive** and **greater than 1**.
 
 
 
• **Sign Convention:** According to the **New Cartesian Sign Convention**, distances measured in the direction of incident light are **positive**, while those measured against it are **negative**. For a concave mirror, the **focal length** is always **negative**.
 
• **Radius of Curvature:** The distance between the pole and the center of curvature is called the **radius of curvature (R)**, and it is equal to twice the focal length (**R = 2f**).
</ul

• **By Roots**: Some plants like **Sweet Potato** and **Dahlia** develop adventitious buds on their roots which grow into new plants.
 
• **By Stems**: Modified stems like **Tubers (Potato)**, **Rhizomes (Ginger and Turmeric)**, and **Bulbs (Onion)** are common natural storage organs used for propagation.
 
• **By Leaves**: Plants like **Bryophyllum** produce adventitious buds along their **leaf margins**; when these leaves fall on moist soil, the buds develop into new plantlets.
 
 
 
• **Artificial Methods of Vegetative Propagation**:
 
 
• **Cutting**: A small part of the stem with nodes is buried in the soil, commonly seen in **Rose, Sugarcane, and Grapes**.
 
• **Grafting**: Joining two different plants (the **scion** and the **stock**) so they grow as a single plant, widely used in **Mango and Citrus fruits**.
 
• **Layering**: A branch of the plant is bent to the ground and covered with soil to induce root formation while still attached to the parent, used for **Jasmine and Lemon**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Genetic Uniformity**: Because there is no **genetic recombination** (which occurs during meiosis in sexual reproduction), there is no **variation**. While this preserves good traits, it also means the entire population is equally **vulnerable to the same diseases** or environmental changes.
 
• **Tissue Culture (Micropropagation)**: This is a modern technique where plant cells or tissues are grown in a **sterile nutrient medium** under controlled conditions. It allows for the rapid production of **disease-free plants** in a very short **time** and limited **space**.
 
• **Survival Rate**: Vegetatively propagated plants often have a **higher survival rate** compared to seedlings because they are already partially developed and have access to the parent's **nutrient reserves** during the initial stages of growth.
 
• **Economic Significance**: This method is vital for the **commercial production** of fruits and flowers where **uniformity in size, taste, and appearance** is required for the market.
</ul

questions.question: What is the colour of the precipitate formed when silver nitrate reacts with sodium chloride?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**White**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The reaction between **Silver Nitrate** (AgNO3) and **Sodium Chloride** (NaCl) is a classic example of a **double displacement reaction**, also known as a **precipitation reaction**.
 
• When an aqueous solution of **Silver Nitrate** is added to an aqueous solution of **Sodium Chloride**, an exchange of ions occurs to form **Silver Chloride** (AgCl) and **Sodium Nitrate** (NaNO3).
 
• **Silver Chloride** is highly **insoluble** in water and settles out of the solution as a solid mass known as a **precipitate**.
 
• The physical observation of this chemical change is the immediate formation of a **curdy white precipitate** of **Silver Chloride**. ***Hence, the statement regarding the white colour is correct.***
 
• The chemical equation for the reaction is: **AgNO3 (aq) + NaCl (aq) → AgCl (s) ↓ + NaNO3 (aq)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Silver Halides and Colours**: 
 
 
• While **Silver Chloride** forms a **white** precipitate, other silver halides exhibit different colours.
 
• **Silver Bromide** (AgBr) forms a **pale yellow** or cream-coloured precipitate.
 
• **Silver Iodide** (AgI) forms a distinct **bright yellow** precipitate.
 
 
 
• **Double Displacement Reaction**: This occurs when the **cations** and **anions** of two different compounds switch places, forming two entirely new compounds. One of these products must be a **precipitate**, a **gas**, or a **molecular compound** like water for the reaction to proceed.
 
• **Solubility Rules**: According to general solubility rules, all **nitrates** (NO3-) are **soluble** in water, while most **silver salts** (except silver nitrate and silver chlorate) are **insoluble**. This explains why AgCl precipitates while NaNO3 remains in the dissolved state.
 
• **Analytical Chemistry**: This specific reaction is widely used as a **qualitative test** to detect the presence of **chloride ions** in a given substance. If the addition of silver nitrate produces a **white** precipitate that is soluble in **dilute ammonia**, the presence of chloride is confirmed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Photolytic Decomposition**: **Silver Chloride** is sensitive to light. When exposed to **sunlight**, the **white** precipitate of **AgCl** decomposes into **grey** metallic **silver** and **chlorine gas**. 
 
• **Equation for Decomposition**: **2AgCl (s) → 2Ag (s) + Cl2 (g)** (in the presence of **UV light**).
 
• **Historical Use**: Due to its light-sensitive nature, silver chloride was fundamentally important in the development of **black-and-white photography** during the **19th century**.
 
• **Laboratory Safety**: Silver nitrate is a strong **oxidizing agent** and can cause **dark stains** on the skin and clothes, which is why it must be handled with care in the **chemistry laboratory**.
</ul

questions.question:
Select the option that is true regarding the following two statements labelled Assertion (A) and Reason (R).

**Assertion (A): **Soap solution appears cloudy.
**Reason (R): **The soap micelles are large enough to scatter light.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Assertion (A)** states that a soap solution appears **cloudy**. This occurs because soap molecules do not form a true solution in water at higher concentrations; instead, they form a **colloidal solution**. *Hence, Assertion (A) is correct.*
 
• **Reason (R)** explains that **soap micelles** are large enough to **scatter light**. In a soap solution, the clusters of molecules, known as micelles, have dimensions typically ranging from **1 to 1000 nanometers**. *Hence, Reason (R) is correct.*
 
• When a beam of light passes through a colloidal soap solution, the **micelles scatter the light** in all directions. This phenomenon is known as the **Tyndall Effect**.
 
• Because the light is scattered rather than passing directly through (as it would in a clear, true solution like salt water), the solution appears **translucent or cloudy** to the naked eye.
 
• Since the scattering of light by these large particles is the direct cause of the visual cloudiness, **Reason (R)** provides a scientifically accurate **explanation for Assertion (A)**. *Hence, both statements are true and R correctly explains A.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of Soap Molecules**:
 
 
• Soap is a **sodium or potassium salt** of long-chain **carboxylic acids** (fatty acids).
 
• Each molecule has two distinct parts: a **hydrophilic (water-loving) head** which is ionic and a **hydrophobic (water-fearing) tail** made of a long hydrocarbon chain.
 
 
 
• **Micelle Formation**:
 
 
• When soap is added to water, the **hydrophobic tails** cluster together to stay away from water, while the **hydrophilic heads** face outward into the water.
 
• This unique orientation results in the formation of spherical aggregates called **micelles**.
 
 
 
• **Colloidal Nature**:
 
 
• A **colloid** is a mixture where one substance consisting of microscopic dispersed particles is suspended throughout another substance.
 
• Unlike **True Solutions** (where particle size is less than **1 nanometer**), colloids have particles large enough to interfere with light but small enough not to settle down under **gravity**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC)**: This is the specific concentration of surfactants above which **micelles** begin to form. Below this concentration, soap acts like a normal electrolyte and the solution may appear clearer.
 
• **Tyndall Effect**: Named after the **19th-century** physicist **John Tyndall**, who first studied the scattering of light by colloidal particles in detail. It is the reason why the **path of light** becomes visible when passing through milk, fog, or a soap solution.
 
• **Cleaning Action**: The cloudiness of the soap solution is also related to its ability to clean. The **hydrophobic center** of the micelle traps **oil and grease**, allowing them to be washed away with water.
 
• **Solubility**: Soap is **soluble** in water, but the formation of large molecular clusters (micelles) changes the optical properties of the resulting mixture from **transparent** to **opaque/cloudy**.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following countries hosted the 8th International Solar Alliance Assembly in October 2025?

__
 
• The **8th Assembly of the International Solar Alliance (ISA)** is slated to be held in **October 2025** in **New Delhi, India**.
 
• The **Assembly** is the **supreme decision-making body** of the **ISA**, in which each **Member Country** is represented to oversee the implementation of the **ISA Framework Agreement**.
 
• As the **host country** and the permanent seat of the **Secretariat**, **India** consistently plays a central role in organizing the annual proceedings to promote **solar energy** globally.
 
• The **8th Assembly** will focus on critical thematic areas such as **solar-pumping systems**, **solar mini-grids**, and the scaling up of **solar rooftops** to achieve **energy transition** targets.
 
• During this session, **Member Countries** will deliberate on **financial mechanisms** to de-risk investments and provide **technical assistance** to the **Least Developed Countries (LDCs)** and **Small Island Developing States (SIDS)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **International Solar Alliance (ISA):**
 
 
• The **ISA** was conceived as a joint effort by **India** and **France** to mobilize efforts against **climate change** through the deployment of **solar energy** solutions.
 
• It was launched by **Prime Minister Narendra Modi** and then-**President François Hollande** on **30 November 2015**, on the sidelines of the **COP21** in **Paris**.
 
• The **ISA** is the first treaty-based international government organization to be headquartered in **India**, specifically at the **National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE)** campus in **Gurugram, Haryana**.
 
• The current **Director General** of the **ISA** is **Dr. Ajay Mathur**, who leads the **Secretariat** in implementing the **ISA's** strategic programs.
 
 
 
• **Vision and Mission:**
 
 
• The **ISA’s** vision is to "**Let us together make the sun brighter**" while its mission is to facilitate **energy access** and **security** worldwide.
 
• The organization aims to mobilize **$1 trillion** (USD) of **investment** in **solar energy** by the **year 2030**.
 
• **Membership:**
 
 
• While initially restricted to **sunshine countries** (those lying between the **Tropic of Cancer** and the **Tropic of Capricorn**), the **ISA** has amended its framework to allow all **Member States** of the **United Nations** to join.
 
• As of **2024**, more than **100 countries** have signed the **ISA Framework Agreement**.

questions.question: In 2025, the Government of India consolidated 29 labour laws into how many labour codes to simplify labour regulations?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**4**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Government of India** initiated a major reform in labour governance by consolidating **29 central labour laws** into **4 comprehensive Labour Codes** to simplify regulations and promote **Ease of Doing Business**.
 
• The four codes resulting from this consolidation are the **Code on Wages, 2019**, the **Industrial Relations Code, 2020**, the **Social Security Code, 2020**, and the **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020**.
 
• This legislative overhaul was designed to replace **archaic and complex laws** dating back to the pre-independence era, ensuring a more **transparent** and **modern** framework for both employers and employees.
 
• The consolidation process aims to provide **universal social security** and **minimum wages** to nearly **50 crore workers** in both the **organized and unorganized sectors**.
 
• The **Ministry of Labour and Employment** spearheaded this transition to reduce **multiplicity of definitions** and **compliance burdens**, which previously hindered industrial growth and job creation. ***Hence, the correct answer is 4.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Code on Wages, 2019:**
 
 
• It was the first code to be passed by **Parliament** in **August 2019**.
 
• It subsumes **4 central laws**: The **Payment of Wages Act, 1936**, the **Minimum Wages Act, 1948**, the **Payment of Bonus Act, 1965**, and the **Equal Remuneration Act, 1976**.
 
• The code introduces a **Floor Wage** to be set by the **Central Government**, ensuring that no state sets a minimum wage lower than this threshold.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Relations Code, 2020:**
 
 
• It consolidates **3 laws**, including the **Trade Unions Act, 1926**, the **Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946**, and the **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947**.
 
• It seeks to streamline the **dispute resolution mechanism** and allows units with up to **300 workers** to retrench or lay off employees without prior government permission, up from the previous limit of **100**.
 
 
 
• **Social Security Code, 2020:**
 
 
• This code integrates **9 laws** such as the **Employees’ Provident Fund Act**, the **Employees’ State Insurance Act**, and the **Maternity Benefit Act**.
 
• For the first time, it brings **gig workers**, **platform workers**, and **unorganized workers** under the ambit of social security schemes like **life insurance** and **disability insurance**.
 
 
 
• **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020:**
 
 
• It subsumes **13 laws** related to **factories**, **mines**, **plantations**, and **construction sites**.
 
• It mandates **free health check-ups** for employees above a certain age and provides for a **national occupational safety and health advisory board**.
 
• The code also formalizes the employment of **inter-state migrant workers** by providing them with **journey allowances** and **ration benefits**.

questions.question: In 2025, according to the Supreme Court, the average waiting period for adopting an infant or young child in India under the legal framework is significant, leading some parents to consider illegal adoptions. What is the approximate average waiting period cited by the Court?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**3.5 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Supreme Court of India**, in recent hearings during **2024** and **2025**, highlighted that the average waiting period for **Prospective Adoptive Parents (PAPs)** to adopt a child through the legal channel is approximately **3.5 years**. ***Hence, the statement regarding the 3.5-year wait is correct.***
 
• A bench led by the **Chief Justice of India** expressed grave concern that such a long gestation period often forces desperate parents to bypass the **Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA)** and resort to **illegal adoptions**.
 
• The court noted that there is a massive imbalance between supply and demand; while over **30,000 PAPs** are registered with **CARA**, only about **2,147 children** were legally available for adoption as of late **2023**.
 
• The **Supreme Court** emphasized that the delay is largely due to the slow process of declaring children "**legally free for adoption**" by **Child Welfare Committees (CWCs)** and administrative bottlenecks at the district level.
 
• Under the **Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015**, the legal process is designed to be rigorous to protect the child's interest, but the procedural delays have inadvertently created a market for **child trafficking**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **CARA (Central Adoption Resource Authority)**:
 
 
• It is a **statutory body** under the **Ministry of Women and Child Development**, Government of India.
 
• It functions as the nodal body for the adoption of Indian children and is mandated to monitor and regulate both **in-country** and **inter-country** adoptions.
 
• **CARA** is the designated central authority under the **Hague Convention on Inter-country Adoption, 1993**, ratified by **India** in **2003**.
 
 
 
• **The Juvenile Justice Act vs. HAMA**:
 
 
• **The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015**: A secular law that allows any person, regardless of religion, to adopt. It provides a comprehensive framework for the rehabilitation of **orphaned, abandoned, and surrendered** children.
 
• **Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act (HAMA), 1956**: Applies to **Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs**. Unlike the **JJ Act**, adoptions under **HAMA** are a private contract between two parties. However, the **Supreme Court** has recently mandated that **HAMA** adoptions must also be registered on the **CARA** portal to ensure child safety.
 
 
 
• **Recent Reforms (2021-2022)**:
 
 
• In **2021**, the **Juvenile Justice Amendment Act** was passed, which empowered **District Magistrates (DMs)** and **Additional District Magistrates (ADMs)** to issue adoption orders instead of civil courts.
 
• The **2022 Adoption Regulations** aimed to simplify the process, but the waiting period for **infants** (below **2 years** of age) remains the highest due to the preference of most **PAPs** for younger children.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Child Welfare Committee (CWC)**: These are district-level bodies that have the sole authority to declare a child "**legally free for adoption**" after conducting due inquiry. Delays at this stage are a primary reason for the **3.5-year** wait.
 
• **SARA (State Adoption Resource Agency)**: This acts as a state-level nodal body to promote and monitor adoption within a particular **State** or **Union Territory**.
 
• **Data Fact**: As per **CARA** reports, the number of annual adoptions in **India** has stagnated around **3,000 to 4,000** per year for the last decade, despite tens of thousands of parents being on the waiting list.
 
• **Types of Children**: A child is **abandoned** if deserted by parents, **orphaned** if both parents are deceased/incapable, and **surrendered** if parents relinquish custody to the **CWC** due to physical, emotional, or social factors.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following banks revised Priority Sector Lending (PSL) guidelines for Small Finance Banks from FY 2025–26, reducing the PSL target to 60% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure (CEOBE), whichever is higher?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Reserve Bank of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** issued a notification in **April 2024** revising the **Priority Sector Lending (PSL)** targets for **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)**.
 
• According to the revised guidelines, the **PSL** target for **Small Finance Banks** will be adjusted to **60%** of **Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC)** or **Credit Equivalent of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure (CEOBE)**, whichever is higher.
 
• This new target of **60%** is a reduction from the previous mandate of **75%**, aimed at aligning the regulatory framework as these banks grow in scale.
 
• The revised guidelines are scheduled to take effect from the **Financial Year (FY) 2025–2026**.
 
• The **RBI** has structured a transition path where the target remains **75%** until **March 31, 2025**, before shifting to the lower threshold in the subsequent year.
 
• This move is part of the **RBI's** broader roadmap to allow eligible **Small Finance Banks** to transition into **Universal Banks**, provided they meet specific performance and capital criteria.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Priority Sector Lending (PSL):**
 
 
• **PSL** is a mechanism used by the **RBI** to ensure that specific sectors of the economy receive adequate credit.
 
• The **eight** primary sectors include **Agriculture**, **Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs)**, **Export Credit**, **Education**, **Housing**, **Social Infrastructure**, **Renewable Energy**, and **Others**.
 
• While **SFBs** are now moving toward a **60%** target, **Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs)** generally have a **PSL** target of **40%**.
 
 
 
• **Small Finance Banks (SFBs):**
 
 
• These banks were established based on the recommendations of the **Nachiket Mor Committee** to promote **financial inclusion**.
 
• They primarily cater to small business units, small and marginal farmers, and micro and small industries.
 
• Examples of prominent **SFBs** in India include **AU Small Finance Bank**, **Equitas Small Finance Bank**, and **Capital Small Finance Bank**.
 
 
 
• **Universal Bank Transition:**
 
 
• For an **SFB** to transition into a **Universal Bank**, it must have a minimum **Net Worth** of **Rs. 1,000 crore**.
 
• The bank must also have a **scheduled status** and a satisfactory track record of at least **five years** of operation.
 
• The **shares** of the bank must be **listed** on a recognized stock exchange for the transition to be considered.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **ANBC and CEOBE:** **Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC)** represents the total credit provided by the bank after specific adjustments, while **CEOBE** measures the risk associated with **off-balance sheet** items like guarantees and letters of credit.
 
• **Loan Portfolio Mandate:** **Small Finance Banks** are required to ensure that at least **50%** of their loan portfolio comprises loans up to **Rs. 25 lakh** to maintain their focus on small borrowers.
 
• **Capital Adequacy:** These banks are required to maintain a minimum **Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR)** of **15%** on a continuous basis, as per **RBI** norms.
 
• **Regulatory Authority:** The **Reserve Bank of India**, established on **April 1, 1935**, under the **RBI Act, 1934**, holds the primary authority to regulate the Indian banking system and set **monetary policy**.

• **PathGenie** is a state-of-the-art computational software launched by the **Ministry of Science and Technology** in **2025** to revolutionize the medical research landscape.
 
• The primary objective of this platform is to **accelerate the process of drug discovery**, significantly cutting down the time required to move from the laboratory concept to clinical application. ***Hence, option 1 is the correct purpose.***
 
• It utilizes advanced **Artificial Intelligence (AI)** and **Machine Learning (ML)** algorithms to predict how different chemical compounds will interact with biological targets.
 
• By using **predictive modeling**, PathGenie helps researchers identify potential **lead compounds** and optimize their chemical structures with high precision before physical synthesis begins.
 
• The software is designed to handle **high-throughput screening**, allowing scientists to analyze millions of molecular combinations in a fraction of the time taken by traditional methods.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Drug Discovery Cycle**: Historically, developing a new drug takes approximately **10 to 12 years** and involves massive financial investment. Tools like **PathGenie** aim to reduce this window to improve **healthcare accessibility**.
 
• **In-Silico Testing**: This refers to research performed on a computer or via computer simulation. **PathGenie** facilitates **in-silico** trials, which minimize the initial need for **animal testing** and reduce ethical concerns in the early research stages.
 
• **Ministry of Science and Technology**: In **India**, this ministry oversees departments such as the **Department of Biotechnology (DBT)** and the **Department of Science and Technology (DST)**, both of which are pivotal in driving **biopharmaceutical innovation**.
 
• **Bioinformatics**: This is the interdisciplinary field that develops methods and software tools for understanding biological data, especially large and complex data sets. **PathGenie** is a prime example of **bioinformatics** application in the modern era.
 
• **Economic Impact**: By streamlining the **pre-clinical phase**, the software helps in lowering the overall cost of **R&D (Research and Development)**, which can eventually lead to more affordable **life-saving medicines** for the public.

• **Target Identification**: The first step in **drug discovery** where a specific **protein** or **gene** involved in a disease is identified as a target for the drug.
 
• **Lead Optimization**: The process of refining a **chemical lead** to improve its **potency**, reduce side effects, and ensure it can be safely absorbed by the human body.
 
• **Data Security**: Since **PathGenie** manages sensitive molecular data, it incorporates high-level **encryption** and **cloud security** to protect the **intellectual property** of Indian scientists and research institutions.
 
• **2025 Milestone**: The launch of this software in **2025** aligns with the national goal of achieving **Atmanirbhar Bharat** (Self-reliant India) in the **pharmaceutical** and **biotechnology** sectors.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following authorities in India issued new directives aimed at regulating asbestos exposure and its disposal in October 2025?

The correct answer is __**National Green Tribunal (NGT)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **National Green Tribunal (NGT)** is the principal judicial body in India responsible for environmental protection. In **October 2025**, it issued comprehensive new directives to strictly regulate the handling and disposal of **asbestos** to mitigate health risks. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***

• The **NGT** emphasized the need for specialized **disposal protocols** for **asbestos-containing materials (ACM)**, particularly during the demolition of old industrial and residential structures.

• The directives mandate that the **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)** and **State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs)** must monitor **air quality** near asbestos processing units to ensure **fiber concentration** remains within safe limits. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect as CPCB is an executing body here, not the primary directive issuer in this context.***

• The tribunal also highlighted the **"Polluter Pays Principle"**, stating that industries failing to manage **asbestos waste** scientifically would face heavy environmental compensation fines.

• While the **High Court of Delhi** and the **Supreme Court of India** often hear environmental litigations, the specific administrative directives for asbestos regulation in **October 2025** were spearheaded by the **NGT**. ***Hence, statements 2 and 4 are incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Asbestos and Health Hazards:**

• **Asbestos** is a group of six naturally occurring silicate minerals made of microscopic **fibers**. It was widely used in **construction** for its **fire-resistant** and **insulating** properties.

• Inhalation of these fibers can lead to serious conditions such as **Asbestosis** (scarring of the lungs), **Lung Cancer**, and **Mesothelioma** (a rare cancer of the chest lining).

• Due to these risks, over **60 countries** have banned the use of all forms of asbestos, though **Chrysotile (white asbestos)** is still used in **India** for roofing and piping under controlled conditions.

• **National Green Tribunal (NGT):**

• Established on **18th October 2010** under the **National Green Tribunal Act, 2010**.

• Its primary **objective** is the effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to **environmental protection** and conservation of forests.

• The **Principal Bench** of the NGT is located in **New Delhi**, with regional benches in **Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, and Chennai**.

• **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB):**

• A statutory organization constituted in **September 1974** under the **Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974**.

• It provides technical services to the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC)** and coordinates the activities of **State Boards**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Hazardous Waste Management:** The disposal of asbestos in India is governed by the **Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016**.

• **Waste Disposal Methods:** The **October 2025** directives specifically advocate for the **Secure Landfill** method, where asbestos waste is wrapped in **leak-proof** packaging and buried at depths that prevent **fiber release** into the atmosphere.

• **Constitutional Provision:** Environmental litigation in India is often supported by **Article 21** (Right to Life) and **Article 48A** (Protection and improvement of environment) of the **Constitution of India**.
</ul

questions.question: Who gave assent to the Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2025, making it a law?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**President of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Under the **Constitution of India**, specifically **Article 111**, no bill passed by the **Parliament** can become a law (an Act) without the formal **assent** of the **President of India**.
 
• The **Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2025**, followed the standard legislative procedure where it was introduced, debated, and passed by both the **Lok Sabha** (Lower House) and the **Rajya Sabha** (Upper House) before being sent to the **President**.
 
• The **President of India** acts as the final authority in the legislative process; once the signature is affixed, the bill is transformed into a **Statute** or **Law**.
 
• Following the **Presidential assent**, the law is published in the **Official Gazette of India** by the **Legislative Department** of the **Ministry of Law and Justice**.
 
• The **President** has the power to grant assent, withhold assent, or return the bill (if it is not a Money Bill) for reconsideration, but once passed again by both houses, the **President** must give assent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2025:**
 
 
• This legislative move aims to amend the **Waqf Act, 1995**, which governs the management and administration of **Waqf properties** (properties dedicated for religious or charitable purposes under Islamic law) in **India**.
 
• The **2025 amendment** focuses on increasing **transparency**, improving the **audit** of accounts, and ensuring better **representation** for women and non-Muslims in **Waqf Boards**.
 
• It sought to redefine the powers of the **Waqf Board** regarding the declaration of a property as "Waqf" and enhanced the role of the **District Collector** in the verification process.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Vice President:**
 
 
• The **Vice President of India** serves as the **Ex-officio Chairman** of the **Rajya Sabha**. While they preside over the passage of the bill in the Upper House, they do not possess the constitutional authority to grant final assent to a bill.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Prime Minister:**
 
 
• The **Prime Minister** is the head of the **Government** and leads the **Cabinet** that proposes legislation. However, the **Prime Minister** does not sign bills into law; this is a **sovereign function** performed by the **Head of State** (the President).
 
 
 
• **Role of the Chief Justice of India (CJI):**
 
 
• The **Chief Justice of India** is the head of the **Judiciary**. The judiciary's role is to interpret laws and check their **constitutionality** (Judicial Review), but they have no role in the **assent** or enactment phase of the legislative process.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC):** In many instances involving complex legislation like the **Waqf (Amendment) Bill**, a **JPC** is formed to examine the provisions in detail before the final vote in **Parliament**.
 
• **Article 111 Options:** The **President** can exercise three options: **Assent** (signing), **Withhold** (pocket veto/absolute veto), or **Return** (suspensive veto). For the **Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2025** to become law, the "Assent" option was exercised.
 
• **Ministry of Minority Affairs:** This is the nodal ministry responsible for the administration of **Waqf** matters at the **Union** level in **India**.
 
• **Central Waqf Council:** Established in **1964**, it is a statutory body that advises the **Central Government** on matters concerning the working of **State Waqf Boards**.
</ul

• The **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)** officially launched the **BHARATPOL** portal in **January 2025** to revolutionize how law enforcement agencies communicate and share data.

• **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI):**
 
 
• Established in **1963**, the **CBI** is India’s premier investigating agency and functions under the **Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions**.
 
• It derives its investigative powers from the **Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946**.
 
• The **CBI** represents **India** as the **National Central Bureau (NCB)** of **INTERPOL**, coordinating with **196 member countries** to tackle **transnational crimes**.
 
 
 
• **Intelligence Bureau (IB):**
 
 
• The **IB** is India’s internal intelligence agency, primarily responsible for domestic security, **counter-intelligence**, and monitoring internal threats.
 
• It functions under the **Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)** and is considered one of the oldest intelligence organizations in the world.
 
 
 
• **National Investigation Agency (NIA):**
 
 
• The **NIA** was formed in **2009** following the **2008 Mumbai terror attacks** to investigate **terrorism-related** offenses across the country.
 
• It operates under the **NIA Act, 2008**, and has the authority to investigate cases across states without needing special permission from state governments.
 
 
 
• **Research and Analysis Wing (RAW):**
 
 
• Established in **1968**, **RAW** is India’s foreign intelligence agency focused on gathering **external intelligence** and conducting counter-terrorism operations outside Indian borders.
 
• It reports directly to the **Prime Minister** through the **National Security Adviser (NSA)**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Transnational Crime Coordination:** The **BHARATPOL** portal specifically targets **transnational organized crimes**, including **human trafficking**, **drug smuggling**, and **cybercrimes** that have international footprints.
 
• **Digital Integration:** The portal integrates with **INTERPOL’s I-24/7** global police communication system, ensuring that even a local police officer in a remote district can receive alerts about **global criminals**.
 
• **Data Modernization:** This initiative is part of the broader **Digital India** mission to modernize the **security infrastructure** and ensure **data-driven policing** to improve the conviction rate in complex cases.
 
• **NCB-New Delhi:** As the host of **NCB-New Delhi**, the **CBI** uses **BHARATPOL** to empower state police agencies by providing them access to **19 specialized databases** maintained by **INTERPOL**, such as those for **stolen travel documents** and **fingerprints**.
</ul

__
 
• The **Indus Waters Treaty (IWT)** is a water-distribution treaty between **India** and **Pakistan**, brokered by the **World Bank** (formerly the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development).
 
• In **2025**, India took significant diplomatic steps to review and modify the treaty, following a formal notice issued in **late 2024**. The move was prompted by **Pakistan’s** persistent objections to Indian hydroelectric projects, specifically the **Kishanganga** and **Ratle** projects in **Jammu and Kashmir**.
 
• The treaty was signed in **Karachi** on **September 19, 1960**, by the then Indian Prime Minister **Jawaharlal Nehru** and Pakistani President **Ayub Khan**. ***Hence, the correct option is Indus.***
 
• Under the original terms of the treaty, the waters of the three **Eastern Rivers**—the **Ravi**, **Beas**, and **Sutlej**—were allocated to **India** for unrestricted use.
 
• The waters of the three **Western Rivers**—the **Indus**, **Jhelum**, and **Chenab**—were allocated to **Pakistan**, with **India** permitted "limited" non-consumptive use, such as for power generation and agriculture.
 
• The dispute escalated in **2025** because **Pakistan** approached the **Permanent Court of Arbitration** in **The Hague**, while **India** insisted on a **Neutral Expert** mechanism, leading to a "graded" suspension or formal call for modification of the 64-year-old pact by the **Government of India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Shimla Agreement:**
 
 
• Signed on **July 2, 1972**, by **Indira Gandhi** and **Zulfikar Ali Bhutto** following the **1971 Indo-Pak War**.
 
• It converted the cease-fire line of **1948** into the **Line of Control (LoC)** and emphasized the resolution of differences through bilateral negotiations.
 
 
 
• **Tashkent Declaration:**
 
 
• A peace agreement signed on **January 10, 1966**, between **India** and **Pakistan** to end the **1965 War**.
 
• It was brokered by the **Soviet Union** in **Tashkent** (now in Uzbekistan) and signed by **Lal Bahadur Shastri** and **Ayub Khan**.
 
 
 
• **Ganga Water Treaty:**
 
 
• This is a bilateral treaty signed in **1996** between **India** and **Bangladesh** for the sharing of the **Ganga** waters at **Farakka**.
 
• It is not related to **Pakistan**; it has a **30-year** validity period and is due for renewal or review in **2026**.
 
 
 
• **Article XII (3) of IWT:**
 
 
• This specific article of the **Indus Waters Treaty** allows for the provisions of the treaty to be modified from time to time by a duly ratified treaty concluded for that purpose between the **two Governments**.
 
• India invoked its right to seek modifications in **2023-2025** due to changes in **demographic** and **environmental** circumstances.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Permanent Indus Commission (PIC):** The treaty established a permanent body with commissioners from both countries who meet at least **once a year** to discuss technical issues and manage water rights.
 
• **World Bank Role:** While the **World Bank** is a signatory to the treaty, its role is primarily limited to procedural matters and appointing a **Neutral Expert** in case of "differences."
 
• **Kishanganga Project:** A **330 MW** hydroelectric project on the **Kishanganga River** (a tributary of the **Jhelum**) which has been a primary point of contention between the two nations since **2007**.
 
• **Ratle Hydroelectric Plant:** An **850 MW** run-of-the-river power station currently under construction on the **Chenab River** in the **Kishtwar district** of **Jammu and Kashmir**.
